entities.summary:
The Greek language has been a cornerstone of intellectual and practical discourse across civilizations for millennia. Emerging from the Proto-Indo-European branch, Greek evolved into a distinct language with its own alphabet, grammar, and literature.


The earliest written records of Greek date back to around 750 BCE, with the oldest surviving texts being the Epic Cycle and the Iliad. As the language spread throughout the Mediterranean, Greek became a lingua franca, facilitating cultural exchange and the transmission of ideas. The works of Aristotle, Plato, and other Greek philosophers had a profound impact on Western philosophy and science.


Greek also played a crucial role in the development of Western theater, with the works of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides influencing the genre for centuries to come. The language's impact can be seen in the many languages that have borrowed words and phrases from Greek, including English.


In the Hellenistic period, Greek became the language of the ancient world, with many rulers and intellectuals adopting it as their primary language. The spread of Greek was facilitated by the conquests of Alexander the Great, who spread Greek culture and language throughout his vast empire. As a result, Greek became a key factor in the transmission of knowledge and culture from the ancient world to the modern era.


Today, Greek remains an important language, with millions of speakers around the world. It continues to be studied and spoken in many parts of the world, and its legacy can be seen in many areas of modern life, from science and philosophy to literature and art.


Despite its modern usage, Greek is a language with a rich and complex history, shaped by the cultural and linguistic exchange of the ancient world. Its impact on Western civilization has been profound, and it remains an essential part of our cultural heritage.
